idiom_name: pure enhancer function: component => enhanced component, applied once at the composition site
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: write one pure function per concern that takes the component (plus optional configuration) and returns a new component with the same interface - it renders the wrapped component and merges its injected inputs with everything it passes through. Apply the enhancer once, where the component is defined or exported, never inside a render path, so the enhanced component keeps a stable identity; keep single-input enhancers so that they compose (compose/flowRight) and their order is explicit. The enhancer owns the concern's state and lifecycle, while the wrapped component stays unaware and independently usable, and every boundary concern (refs, static members, identity, optional interfaces) must be forwarded deliberately instead of assumed.
code_sketch:
enhance(configure?) -> (Component) => Enhanced

Enhanced(props):
    concern_state = owned by the enhancer        # subscription, permission, flag, theme
    return Component(merge(injected(concern_state), passthrough(props)))

# once, at the definition site:
Export = compose(withRouter, withAnalytics(Component))   # order is explicit
# never: Enhanced = enhance(Component) inside the render path (a new type each render)
pitfalls: Applying the enhancer inside a render path: a new component type is produced on every render, which remounts the subtree and loses its state.
Mutating the wrapped component instead of wrapping it, so the enhancement is invisible to other enhancers and to the wrapped component's own users.
Assuming boundary features survive wrapping: refs, static members and optional interfaces must be forwarded explicitly.

TypeScript inference collapse in multi-HOC generic chains: a deeply nested generic HOC (T extends {}, then another HOC wrapping it) can infer T as unknown or never, especially with intersection types; work around with explicit type parameters at the call site or break the chain into named intermediate types.

Memory leaks from uncleaned subscriptions: an enhancer that subscribes to an external source (store, WebSocket, event bus) and does not unsubscribe on unmount will hold the subscription open for the lifetime of the enhanced component instance; always return a cleanup function from useEffect or implement componentWillUnmount.

Testing the wrapped component in isolation is opaque: a unit test written against the enhanced export cannot see what props the enhancer injects or what it strips; the pattern requires exporting the unwrapped component as a named export alongside the enhanced default export.

Context is the better primitive for ambient cross-cutting data: when the same value (user, theme, locale) is needed by many components at unpredictable depths, a Context provider + useContext hook carries it with zero wrapper nodes, while an enhancer creates a node even for components that do not consume the value.

The React Compiler (autopratic) cannot see through wrapper layers to apply context-specific optimizations: memo, value equality and return-type specialization are all degraded when a component is wrapped, making enhancers a partial performance regression relative to equivalent hooks.

Silent API breakage when a wrapped class component is refactored to a function: any enhancer relying on class-component lifecycle (componentDidMount, componentWillReceiveProps) will silently stop running the lifecycle hook on the wrapped function component unless the enhancer is also updated.

Enhancer ordering in a compose chain has subtle semantics: withAuth(withTheme(Component)) is not the same as withTheme(withAuth(Component)) when both inject props — the outer enhancer sees the inner enhancer's injected props in its render, which can cause incorrect initialisation or extra renders if the enhancers are order-sensitive.

Mutating-HOC temptation: an enhancer that patches the wrapped component (or relies on inheritance) risks name clashes, silently overrides earlier enhancers in the chain and fails on function components — the React documentation explicitly bans this variant; wrap, never mutate.

Reactivity wraps must be innermost: MobX requires observer to be applied first (the innermost HOC/decorator) so the re-render subscription tracks the real render; placing it outside another prop-injecting HOC can miss observables read through the injected props layer.

Composition pipelines hide the data flow: an enhance(compose(withState, mapProps, pure, ...)) stack reads like a declaration but renames, maps and drops props at each step, so what the inner component finally receives must be reconstructed by hand — a maintenance trap at scales where a hook keeps the flow explicit.
sources: React documentation (legacy), 'Higher-Order Components' — canonical rules for the generic form: HOCs are pure functions, must not mutate the wrapped component, must not be applied inside render, and refs/statics/displayName caveats. URL: https://legacy.reactjs.org/docs/higher-order-components.html
MobX official documentation, 'React integration' — observer HOC usage and the apply-observer-first (innermost) composition rule. URL: https://mobx.js.org/react-integration.html
